readings.c1s1:
¶
{{smaller block|We are so now ordered and so straitly watched, that ''unneaths'' our servants dare do anything for us.
{{right|''Bp. Ridley'', in Bradford’s Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 174.}}}}

'''unebriate''' (un-ē′bri-āt), ''a.'' Unintoxicating; also, unintoxicated. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|There were . . . ''unebriate'' liquors, pressed from cooling fruits.
{{right|''Bulwer'', My Novel, IV. xvii. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unedge''' (un-ej′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''edge''<sup>1</sup>.] To deprive of the edge; blunt.
{{smaller block|<poem>Here our weapons,
And bodies that were made for shining brass,
Are both ''unedg’d.''</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Valentinian, i. 3.}}}}

'''unedible''' (un-ed′i-bl), ''a.'' Inedible. ''Hugh Miller.'' [Rare.]

'''unedifying''' (un-ed′i-fī-ing), ''a.'' Not edifying; not improving to the mind. ''Boyle.''

'''uneducate<sup>1</sup>†''' (un-ed′ū-kāt), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''educate, a.''] Not educated. ''Solyman and Perseda.''

'''uneducate<sup>2</sup>''' (un-ed̮′ū-kāt), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''educate, v.''] To deprive of education; reverse or annul what has been done by way of educating or training. ''H. Spencer'', Social Statics, p. 388.

'''uneducated''' (un-ed̮′ū-kā-ted), ''a.'' Not educated; illiterate.

'''uneffectual''' (un-e-fek′t̮ū-a̤l), ''a.'' Ineffectual. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The glow-worm shows the matin to be near,
And ’gins to pale his ''uneffectual'' fire.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 5. 90.}}}}

'''unelastic''' (un-ē-las′tik), ''a.'' Inelastic. ''The Engineer'', LXXI. 72. [Rare.]

'''unembarrassed''' (un-em-bar′ạst), ''a.'' Not embarrassed, in any sense.

'''unembodied''' (un-em-bod′id), ''a.'' '''1.''' Disembodied. ''Byron'', When Coldness Wraps. [Rare.] —'''2.''' Not embodied; not collected into a body: as, ''unembodied'' militia. ''Imp. Dict.'' [Rare.]

'''unemotional''' (un-ē-mō′shọn-a̤l), ''a.'' Not emotional; free from or unaccompanied by an exhibition of emotion or feeling; impassive; not inducing emotion: as, an ''unemotional'' person; an ''unemotional'' book.
{{smaller block|This little book [“Nature”] met with a very ''unemotional'' reception.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Emerson (Amer. Men of Letters, p. 91).}}}}

'''unemotionally''' (un-ē-mō′shọn-a̤l-i), ''adv.'' In an unemotional manner; impassively.

'''unemotioned''' (un-ē-mō′shọnd), ''a.'' Free from emotion; impassive. ''Godwin'', Mandeville, iii. 98. [Rare.]

'''unemployed''' (un-em-ploid′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not employed; having no work or employment.
{{smaller block|Men sour with poverty and ''unemployed.'' {{right|''Addison.''}}
The fact is, Africa is a nation of the ''unemployed.''
{{right|''The Speaker'', May 31, 1890.}}}}
'''2.''' Not in use: as, ''unemployed'' capital or money.
{{smaller block|An overflow of ''unemployed'' energy and vivacity.
{{right|''M. C. Tyler'', Life of Patrick Henry, p. 16.}}}}

'''unenchanted''' (un-en-chȧn′ted), ''a.'' Not enchanted; that cannot be enchanted. ''Milton'', Comus, l. 395.

'''unenclosed,''' ''a.'' See ''uninclosed.''

'''unencumber, unincumber''' (un-en-, un-in-kum′bėr), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''encumber.''] To free from encumbrance; disencumber.

'''unencumberedness''' (un-en-kum′bėrd-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unencumbered. ''The Atlantic'', LXVII. 182. [Rare.]

'''unendeared''' (un-en-dērd′), ''a.'' Not attended with endearment. ''Milton'', P. L., iv. 766.

'''unended''' (un-en′ded), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unended'', < AS. ''ungeended;'' as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''ended.''] Endless; infinite.

'''unendingness''' (un-en′ding-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unending.

'''unendurable''' (un-en-dūr′a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not to be endured; intolerable.

'''unendurably''' (un-en-dūr′a̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an unendurable manner; intolerably.

'''unengaged''' (un-en-gājd′), ''a.'' Not engaged, in any sense.

'''un-English''' (un-ing′glish), ''a.'' Not English. {{smaller|(''a'') Not characteristic of Englishmen; opposed in character, feeling, etc., to what is English. (''b'') Not properly belonging to, or not in accord with the usages of, the English language.}}

'''un-Englished''' (un-ing′glisht), ''a.'' Not translated or rendered into English. ''Bp. Hall'', Honour of the Married Clergy.

'''unenlightened''' (un-en-lī′tnd), ''a.'' Not enlightened; not mentally or morally illuminated; also, not proceeding from or marked by mental or moral enlightenment: as, ''unenlightened'' zeal.

'''unenthralled''' (un-en-thrâld′), ''a.'' Not enslaved; not reduced to thraldom. ''Milton'', Eikonoklastes.

¶
'''unequal''' (un-ē′kwa̤l), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Not equal; not of the same size, length, breadth, quantity, quality, strength, talents, age, station, etc.
{{smaller block|To shape my legs of an ''unequal'' size.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iii. 2. 159.}}}}
'''2.''' Inadequate; insufficient; inferior: as, his strength was ''unequal'' to the task.
{{smaller block|<poem>Atlas becomes ''unequal'' to his freight,
And almost faints beneath the glowing weight.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., ii.}}
<poem>The Day
''Unequal'' to the Godhead’s Attributes
Various, and Matter copious of your Songs.</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', Second Hymn of Callimachus.}}}}
'''3.''' Not balanced or matched; disproportioned; one-sided; hence, inequitable; unfair; unjust; partial.
{{smaller block|<poem>To punish me for what you make me do
Seems much ''unequal''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., ii. 5. 101.}}
<poem>We play ''unequal'' game,
Whene’er we shoot by Fancy’s aim!</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Rokeby, i. 31.}}}}
'''4.''' Not equable; not uniform; irregular: as, ''unequal'' pulsations.
{{smaller block|I have called him the most original and the most ''unequal'' of living poets.
{{right|''Stedman'', Vict. Poets, p. 338.}}}}

readings.c3s2:
¶
'''unequitably''' (un-ek′wi-ta-bli), ''adv.'' Inequitably. ''Secker'', Charge to Clergy of Oxford (1750).

'''unequity†''' (un-ek′wi̤-ti), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unequitie''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''equity''. Cf. ''iniquity''.] Want of equity; inequity; iniquity. ''Wyclif'', Rom. iii. 5.

'''unequivocal''' (un-ē-kwiv′ō-kal), ''a.'' Not equivocal, in any sense. ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|Plain, unambiguous, unmistakable. See ''obscure''.}}

'''unequivocally''' (un-ē-kwiv′ọ̄-ka̤l-i), ''adv.'' In an unequivocal manner.

'''unequivocalness''' (un-ē-kwiv′ọ̄-kal-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unequivocal.

'''unerrable†''' (un-ėr′a̤-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of erring; infallible. ''Sheldon'', Mirror of Antichrist (1616), p. 142.

'''unerrableness†''' (un-ėr′a̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' Incapacity of error. ''Decay of Christian Piety''.

'''unerring''' (un-ėr′ing), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not missing the mark; certain: as, an ''unerring'' aim.
{{smaller block|<poem>Diana taught him all her silvan arts,
To bend the bow, and aim ''unerring'' darts.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, v. 68.}}}}
'''2.''' Committing no mistake; incapable of error; infallible: as, the ''unerring'' wisdom of God. ''Jer. Taylor'', Dissuasive from Popery.

'''unerringly''' (un-ėr′ing-li), ''adv.'' In an unerring manner; without error, mistake, or failure; infallibly. ''Locke'', Human Understanding, ii. 9.

'''unescapable''' (un-es-kā′pa̤-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be escaped. ''Ruskin.''

'''uneschewable†''' (un-es-chö′a̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ME. ''uneschuable''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''eschew'' + ''-able''.] Unavoidable.
readings.c3s4:
or not of absolute necessity: as, forms are among the ''unessentials'' of religion.

¶
'''unestablish''' (un-es-tab′lish), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''establish''.] To deprive of establishment; disestablish. ''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xxvii. [Rare.]

See ''temperament.''—'''Unequal voices,''' in ''music'', properly, voices of different quality or compass; but the term is often used in the sense of ''mixed voices''.—'''Unequal wings,''' in ''entom.'', wings of which the anterior pair are longer or shorter than the posterior, generally the former.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' One not equal to another in station, power, ability, age, or the like. ''Milton'', P. L., vi. 453. [Rare.]

'''unequalable†''' (un-ē′kwal-ạ-bl), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''equal'' + ''-able''.] Not capable of being equaled; not capable of being matched or paralleled; matchless; peerless. ''Boyle'', Works, I. 282.

'''unequaled, unequalled''' (un-ē′kwald), ''a.'' Not to be equaled; unparalleled; unrivaled. ''Milton'', P. L., ix. 983.='''Syn.''' {{smaller|Unmatched, matchless, unexampled, peerless.}}

'''unequally''' (un-ē′kwạl-i), ''adv.'' Not equally.
{{smaller block|''Unequally'' yoked together.{{right|2 Cor. vi. 14.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Unequally pinnate leaf.''' See ''pinnate.''}}

'''unequalness''' (un-ē′kwạl-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unequal; inequality. ''Sir W. Temple'', Essay on Poetry.

'''unequitable''' (un-ek′wi-tạ-bl), ''a.'' Inequitable. ''A. Tucker.''

'''unequitably''' (un-ek′wi-ta-bli), ''adv.'' Inequitably. ''Secker'', Charge to Clergy of Oxford (1750).

'''unequity†''' (un-ek′wi̤-ti), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unequitie''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''equity''. Cf. ''iniquity''.] Want of equity; inequity; iniquity. ''Wyclif'', Rom. iii. 5.

'''unequivocal''' (un-ē-kwiv′ō-kal), ''a.'' Not equivocal, in any sense. ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|Plain, unambiguous, unmistakable. See ''obscure''.}}

'''unequivocally''' (un-ē-kwiv′ọ̄-ka̤l-i), ''adv.'' In an unequivocal manner.

'''unequivocalness''' (un-ē-kwiv′ọ̄-kal-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unequivocal.

'''unerrable†''' (un-ėr′a̤-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of erring; infallible. ''Sheldon'', Mirror of Antichrist (1616), p. 142.

'''unerrableness†''' (un-ėr′a̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' Incapacity of error. ''Decay of Christian Piety''.

'''unerring''' (un-ėr′ing), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not missing the mark; certain: as, an ''unerring'' aim.
{{smaller block|<poem>Diana taught him all her silvan arts,
To bend the bow, and aim ''unerring'' darts.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, v. 68.}}}}
'''2.''' Committing no mistake; incapable of error; infallible: as, the ''unerring'' wisdom of God. ''Jer. Taylor'', Dissuasive from Popery.

'''unerringly''' (un-ėr′ing-li), ''adv.'' In an unerring manner; without error, mistake, or failure; infallibly. ''Locke'', Human Understanding, ii. 9.

'''unescapable''' (un-es-kā′pa̤-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be escaped. ''Ruskin.''

'''uneschewable†''' (un-es-chö′a̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ME. ''uneschuable''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''eschew'' + ''-able''.] Unavoidable. {{smaller block|An ''uneschuable'' byndynge togydere.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, v. prose 1.}}}}

'''uneschewably†''' (un-es-chö′a̤-bli), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''uneschuably''; < ''uneschewable'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] Unavoidably.

{{smaller block|They ben to comyn ''uneschwably''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, v. prose 3.}}}}

'''unespied''' (un-es-pīd′), ''a.'' Not espied; not discovered; not seen. ''Spenser'', Present State of Ireland.

'''unessayed''' (un-e-sād′), ''a.'' Not essayed; unattempted. ''Milton'', Eikonoklastes.

'''unessence''' (un-es′e̤ns), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''essence''.] To deprive of essence or distinctive characteristics. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Not only does truth, in . . . long intervals, ''unessence'' herself, but (what is harder) one cannot venture a crude fiction, for the fear that it may ripen into a truth upon the voyage.
{{right|''Lamb'', Essays of Elia, p. 178.}}}}

'''unessential''' (un-e-sen′shal), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Not essential; not constituting the essence or essential part; inessential; not of prime importance.

{{smaller block|The ''unessential'' parts of Christianity.
{{right|''Addison'', Freeholder.}}
Sundry ''unessential'' points of church order.
{{right|''H. B. Smith'', Christian Theology, p. 593.}}}}
'''2.''' Void of real being.
{{smaller block|<poem>The void profound
Of ''unessential'' night.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 438.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' Something not constituting essence, or not of absolute necessity: as, forms are among the ''unessentials'' of religion.

'''unestablish''' (un-es-tab′lish), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''establish''.] To deprive of establishment; disestablish. ''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xxvii. [Rare.]<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
